The new mail-in ballot procedure isn’t something to be afraid of. 

It works like this:  

1. The state provides a list of the ballots they intend to mail out.  

2. USPS assigns a unique barcode to each.  

3. When the ballot is mailed out, this barcode is scanned to ensure uniqueness and that it matches. If there is no match or it’s a duplicate, it is not delivered.  

4. When the voter mails the ballot back, the USPS scans it again and checks to make sure it matches what went out and isn’t a duplicate. Any ballots that don’t match won’t be delivered.  

5. This is all done on the exterior envelope. The USPS isn’t determining eligibility or deciding who gets a ballot. They can’t see the actual votes. 

They are essentially just ensuring there are no duplicates, that the number mailed in isn’t greater than the number mailed out, and that the person mailing one in was the same person who received them.  This is a common sense solution and is completely reasonable.   

Why would anyone oppose it unless their intention is to cheat?

I taught History and English; I am also African American.  Classes in predominately white private schools: one progressive, the other conservatively male where the average grade had 74 white boys to 6 black. Teaching Huck Finn in such environments was a challenge, as the novel shows the impotence of black men more than their power.  We too experienced the N-word discomfort.  My approach was to go over all the issues mentioned; we created a blog where students could write feelings they may not have been comfortable expressing and dialog. We listed racial slurs against all groups; their origin and impact. It went well, culminating in a day of people in costumed characters (Halloween Day class) from the novel analyzing their person.  

But I have now gone beyond the novel to teach more readily books that show these same racial and class themes, but show  black men with power: Nelson Mandela's autobiography, Obama's Dreams from My Father, James Allan McPherson's Pulitzer Prize winning short stories in Elbow Room. I let them contrast the telling of the South's "grandeur" in Gone With the Wind with that of Jubilee.  To the extent we do Huck Finn, it is more about narrative voice (unreliable narrator) and how that can shape a novel by comparing it to Morrison's The Bluest Eye (school children) or the Color Purple's protagonist writing to God.   Otherwise Huck Finn, Native Son, and Invisible Man are relics, freezing the image of black male emasculation in impressionable young minds.

comments.name: David

There's a huge difference between acknowledging the existence of racism (whether in history or in the present) and celebrating and perpetuating it.  A statue honoring a confederate general in a public square extols the cause he fought for.  And, presumably, since public squares are public property, its placement there (at tax-payer expense, no less) represents an official governmental imprimatur for the cause of slavery for which the general fought.  In contrast, placing that same statue in a museum is which it is contextualized, meaning not just providing the history of slavery, the insurrection and secession of the southern states, but also the political goals of the sculptor in attempting to glorify that general and the political context in which the sculpture was commissioned and created, teaches about institutionalized racism, as opposed to perpetuating it.  

A schoolroom is like a museum.  It's a repository of history (and other things worth knowing).  American children are not well served by censoring history, including the prevalence of the word in question in this article (and in Twain's novel).  And if the word and its use are contextualized appropriately, educating students about it and its place in history serve the exact opposite purpose of using the word itself.

Context matters.

https://dbalablog.blogspot.com/2017/06/bill-maher-racist-epithets-contextual.html

I count Huck Finn as one of my favorite works of fiction, and, though I don't recall ever reading it for any of my lit classes, for decades owned a tattered paperback that looked very much like a book bought for a middle school lit class, but never discussed. Maybe they didn't want to, even then at a private school in the 1980s. 
My paperback had an introductory critical essay of some importance, probably by Mencken, possibly Ellison, and incisive on one point: Tom Sawyer has no business in the story other than the important business of selling books. Tom Sawyer was Twain's big seller, and he and the publishers had apparently worked it out that Tom had better show up at some point or people might not buy the incredibly important literature that is the story of Huck and Jim. 
I no longer own my old paperback, but after reading it a good ten times, I can say that the first two thirds of Huck Finn is one of the great stories of the world, and I would encourage its teaching. If its good enough for Ralph Ellison, Hemingway and Toni M, it's then quite necessary for the rest of us who would learn to write our own literature.

**REALLY** enjoyed this essay.
  
I am 75, a retired chemist, and have always read for pleasure.  So perhaps my perspective is interesting.

I first read Huck Finn when I was 8-10 and have reread it several times over the intervening years.  Reread it most recently last year for a book club, where we contrasted Huck Finn and James.  I'm sure that we read it in 11th-grade English, but I don't remember that.
  
Huck Finn is one of my all-time favorite books.  When I was a child, I liked Tom Sawyer better than Huck, but by the time I was in my late teens / early 20's I realized that Huck is by far the better story, with much more interesting and developed characters.
  
Sometime later I came to realize something that no one in this essay has pointed out: Huck is basically still a child.  Jim, despite the way his limitations are portrayed, is basically the parent - the only parent that Huck has.  
  
Also, consider the portrait of American life that Huck paints:

  --the feuds! (I can still recite parts from the story of the 
     Shepherdsons and Grangerfords by heart)
  --the small towns!
  --the grifters!
  
and of course
  
  --the River!
  
All of that tied up into one entertaining package.  
  
A package that challenges and stretches the reader, yes.  It's worth doing what needs to be done - getting rid of the N-word, teaching kids to read dialect, whatever else - to continue to teach Huck Finn to various audiences.

In short, the McKinley Tariff Act of 1890 raised U.S. import duties to nearly 48%, and was partly designed as economic coercion to push Canada toward annexation with the theory being that crippling Canadian exports would make statehood look appealing. It backfired completely. Canadian nationalism surged as citizens rallied around their British identity and rejected annexation outright, Canadian trade pivoted sharply toward Britain as exports were deliberately redirected away from the U.S. market, Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on American agricultural goods which hurt U.S. farmers deeply, some American manufacturers relocated production facilities to Canada to sidestep those retaliatory duties, and the cultural and economic bond between Canada and Britain was significantly strengthened at precisely the moment U.S. policymakers had hoped to weaken it. The act stands today as a classic cautionary tale. Tariff pressure on Canada produced the exact opposite of its intended effect, leaving American consumers paying higher prices at home while losing political and economic ground abroad. Here is the essence of our generalized problem: no one is in charge of "being in charge". Everyone is told to "stay in your lane", do you job and, yes siree, shut-up. "That's above my pay grade" has become standard dodge, so much so that it is featured in common movies and novels.

We face numerous situations where everyone does their assigned jobs, sometimes well, sometimes not, but no one is tasked with the extraordinary, the necessary superceding judgement that says, "Hey, here comes a five alarm fire!"

As Covid19 raised its ugly head across the world, only the president of the United States could have easily assembled a public media response that would have helped calm the waters by explaining the complexities and difficulties of dealing with a novel virus, one that had not been known in humans previously. Unfortunately, the available president was AWOL on the issue, wandering around like a character in a Beckett play, lost in the void. As officials around the WH deferred to his lack of judgement and action, nonsense was allowed to run wild. We are still paying the price for that failure.

Over the last few months, I've been alarmed by the thought that the next big war would involve AI agents trying to destroy the entire modern communications systems. Once wrecked, the population would descend into sustained chaos. Everything we've come to depend on would be gone. 

This is not mere fantasy. Who's in charge of getting ready?

This tactic makes no sense (aside from the obvious illegality of these murders).
When law enforcement agencies normally raid drug suppliers, interdict ground transportation of drugs, or stop seagoing vessels carrying drugs, the people are arrested, and the drugs confiscated. Why? Because the people - low level criminals - can be persuaded to give up information about higher levels of the organization, which can lead to actually shutting down - even if only temporarily - their criminal enterprise. 
And the drugs themselves can be used as evidence against those people at the higher levels. More immediately, the drugs and their containers or packaging may furnish clues about their origin and routes.
So, why this expenditure of expensive weapons to blow to smithereens small boats and people who are unlikely to be the ringleaders in the drug trade? 
If a domestic drug enforcement agency such as the DEA were to conduct raids this way, using large amounts of lethal and destructive weaponry that resulted in the complete loss of all evidence and death of every suspect, one would be well justified in wondering what they were trying to hide. If your local police force raided a drug house and incinerated all of the drugs and paraphernalia without using it as evidence against the criminals, you might well speculate that something fishy was going on.
Is there a reason, besides Hegseth's testosterone-fueled mania, to destroy evidence? What don't they want us to know?

comments.name: TacoTaco
comments.body: We can think of opiate addiction in the US as having three waves. In wave one, in the 19th century morphine (or opium extracts like laudenum) was an ingredient of products prescribed by physicians and in readily available patent medicines. Opium dens, where it was smoked, were brought by Chinese immigants. This all created a smoldering addiction problem. The invention of injectable morphine in the civil war was the spark that turned this into a raging inferno. Everyone was stoned. The Safe Food and Drug Act of 1906 came in response. A key objective of this act was to get opiates out of consumer goods. The second wave was the Vietnam war, when surving soldiers sent to Asia were exposed to readily available heroin, and came home with addiction. By the late 70s we had a war on drugs and medical schools taught the high risks of opiate addiction. Pain was not to be treated aggressively in the more enlightened  schools of the day. The third wave hit in the mid 90s when Purdue pharma managed to bamboozle a new generation of physicians at scale into thinking about pain as "the 5th vital sign" and to treat it aggressively. The rates of addiction skyrocketed. The illicit trade saw the opportunity and moved in to take advantage. After each of these waves, the problems of addiction have hit communities of poverty extremely hard, where they run like festering wounds. The only hope, in my opinion , is to prevent the 4th wave. It is quite difficult for me to believe that the 25th anniversary is almost upon us.  For me, this tragedy still feels very recent, as though I could turn around and touch it.

I was still a teenager, eagerly anticipating my future, on that bright blue morning a quarter century ago.  I woke up in my college dorm and looked out the window and thought how blue and clear the sky was.  My roommate was still asleep.  And then, the news on TV: the World Trade Center towers billowing smoke and fire.  I was terrified that it was the end of the world.  Perhaps I can be forgiven for that, because I was only 19 and no one expects to see mass murder on live television, or anywhere.  A few days later I woke up in the middle of the night, terrified, but unable to name the terror: was just there.

I'm 44 now.  I sometimes think that all the people whose lives were snuffed out 25 years ago next month were meant to interact with us all somehow, that there were people we were all supposed to meet, even briefly, befriend, love, etc., and now we never will. Those terrorists permanently altered the psychic ecosystem of the entire planet, because one person's life touches the next, and the ripples reverberate into eternity.  So much was lost. And the potential for our country was lost, too.  We'll never know whom we could have been, and that is the ultimate tragedy.

As we approach this 25th anniversary, I wish us solace. The dead have already achieved that peace which passeth all understanding.

Where I live, a 11,000 Volt cable was buried inches below the road (it's supposed to be at least 3' below the ground, but hey, no one was looking when they installed the cable). The electric company claimed that they could not bury the cable deeper due to a massive granite formation. 

Rolling vehicular traffic would squeeze the shallow cable and cause breakages. Frequently. Leading to neighborhood power cuts and excavations to re-join the broken cable. These excavations, on a narrow, busy street, would hold up traffic. Major inconvenience. Street scuffles, chaos, madness.

A group of us took it up on ourselves to figure out just where the granite rock began. We dug below the cable, and, lo and behold, inches below the cable, we found a ductile iron water pipe. There was no massive granite formation that made it impossible to dig further; the cable broke because it was getting pinched between the pipe below and vehicular tires above.  

The water and electricity departments argued over who should pay for reburying the pipe and cable deeper. A massive excavation and re-work eventually took place. Both cable and pipe are now at safe depths. Excavations are rarer, traffic has calmed down a notch.

This happened in Bangalore, India, where chaos is normal and government service is expected to be sclerotic. I am both surprised and heartened to know that as modern and developed a city as NYC has the same issue of official ignorance of underground works.

The US already imports magnesium from Canada.  This is for two reasons:

1) Permitting Speed: Establishing new mining or refining operations in the U.S. is notoriously slow, taking an average of 7 to 10 years to secure permits. By comparison, Canada’s streamlined regulatory system averages just 2 years.

2) Cheaper Energy Supply: Refining magnesium is an incredibly energy-intensive process. Canada has readily available and affordable hydroelectric power infrastructure, making metal smelting significantly cheaper than in most parts of the U.S.

It makes more sense for the US to import from an ally than from China, and a lot more sense to work with Canada than to fight with them.

Canada accounts for roughly 24% of U.S. magnesium scrap imports, whereas China supplies approximately 20% of U.S. magnesium scrap imports. However, for primary pure magnesium metal, the U.S. imports 0% from China due to anti-dumping tariffs, relying instead on countries like Israel.

The more immediate danger may be our determination to treat one another as enemies, pouring enormous amounts of national energy into fighting the other half of the country rather than asking what we can accomplish together.

America is a tear down, in need of complete renovation.

To even engage this one needs to acknowledge the race and class dimensions of the challenge, argue the flawed nature of human beings, defend nuanced takes against the reflexive accusation that you’re trivializing suffering, etc. We’re at the very beginning of this political story. is yet dependent on human energy,

When there is a breach, the reactor shuts down and the molten salt solidifies, eliminating the risk of leakage. Don't put your phones in your pants pocket or stuffed purse.  Don't put your laptop in an overstuffed bag.  Keep both phones and laptops in separate compartments in your travel bags and purses, preferably ones with some rigid or semi-rigid stiffeners in the sides.  In purses, the middle most compartment is generally safer.

comments.name: Mark H
comments.body: The thing about open-weight AI models is that developers and users can use one on their own machine, depending upon what their needs are. There are advantages to doing so. First is cost. There are LLM models out there that will run on a smartphone, laptop, or PC without having to purchase additional hardware and that are free to download and use. I have one installed on my PC. I do not have to have a subscription or pay for token use. Second is because I can run one on my PC, it reduces the need to having to build large data centers and infrastructure to support them.  I also run Linux, which is also open source software. The salient facts are that Mr. Lane was Forbes' "editor in chief" and that "in 2016 Lane helped to facilitate the partnership between Forbes Media and Shook Research". Previously, "Lane and Shook developed a friendship in 2011".

Without Lane disclosing the transaction  to Forbes, "private-equity firm PPC Enterprises acquired a majority stake in Shook Research last summer.

And, also unbeknownst to Forbes, "Lane assisted in the Shook Research [majority ownership] sales effort by speaking about the relationship between that company and the magazine during the due diligence stage".

Presumably, Lane gave the prospective acquirer assurances about how solid  and continuing Shook's business relationship with Forbes were, especially with Lane as editor in chief.

And if Lane had any foreknowledge that Shook would "make a payment" to him conditioned on the PPC purchase closing, he could be described as an agent with two masters, Forbes and PPC.

Conspicuously absent from the article is any statement by PPC about whether they knew Lane would be paid if the deal with Shook was completed or about what if anything Lane said during PPC's "due diligence" inquiries about the future durability of the Shook-Forbes "partnership".

Lane describes his actions and omissions an "error in judgment". But depending on the results of a fuller investigation, that could be a monumental understatement.

My mother’s first love is music. As a young girl sent off to boarding school, she found solace in music and as an adult, taught music all her life. 
That passion kept her going till the age of 88, when failing health and hearing loss forced her to retire. She’s 92 now and bedridden, but she had created enduring memories and inculcated in me, a lifelong love for music.

comments.name: Retired in CT
comments.body: Lily was my piano teacher when I was a teenager and she established such a helpful foundation for my playing that, throughout my business career and now in retirement, playing piano and organ is still my greatest joy.  I was delighted to see this article about her this morning and also not surprised to learn she was still actively playing.  She shared with me the same drive that has kept her at the piano all these years; it is difficult to put into words, but I can say it's as though the idea music should be a part of your every day life goes without saying.  With the skills I learned from Lily 50+ years ago, I have a thoroughly engaging avocation in retirement that is self-nourishing.  The largest room in our home is the music room, and I enjoy having musicians of all stripes play for us and our friends.  Just last week we had nearly 100 people here for a performance.  And it all started with Lilly.  When you count up all of her students and audience members over nearly a century, think of how many people the devotion to her craft has reached and how many lives have been improved over that time, even if just a little.  We need many more people in this world like her.

This is a very touching and meaningful story. I am inspired by Ms. Friedman. I believe that while the body ages, the spirit literally does not. Being, consciousness, awareness, spirit, soul, etc., is in the same pristine shape at age 95 that it was at age 9. Ms. Friedman appears to feel this way. 

The literature is very demanding. Beethoven’s Opus 111 is a very challenging work at any age, and not just the extended trills to conclude the second movement. 
I am 65, and I have no plans to retire from my position as Director of Sacred Music at a church.  Afterall, Charles Widor served as organist at Saint-Sulpice in Paris for 63 years. But I know, and I have always known, that the demands of my job as organist, pianist, and conductor, are slight compared to the demands of performing the pianist’s repertoire. Having performed major works of Beethoven, Schumann, Scriabin, etc., I know what is required. And that is why I am in such awe of Ms. Friedman. I cannot imagine doing it in my 90’s, but her story encourages me to persevere. 

Ms. Friedman: Here’s to many more years of an astonishing career. Your story inspires people, like myself, who have not personally met you.

I was 10 years old in 1969. Grew up in Nassau County. The NL championship playoff and World Series were played during the day as baseball was meant to be played. Our fifth grade teacher was a sports nut. She had let us watch the playoffs and World Series during class on the black and white TV that sat on a cart in the front corner of the classroom. So yeah, I was a Mets fan from then on. 
I don't really follow the game anymore. The modern data driven approach along with role specialization has taken all the fun out of it. I can recognize the names of maybe a dozen major league players today. A few of them are Mets. One is a Yankee. One is a Dodger. For what its worth and to the degree of my interest I'm still a Mets fan. And that's whether they are good or not.
